rewriteLast.title: Chapter 6 · The First Doll
rewriteLast.artPrompt: A sunlit clearing beside a log cabin in the Laughing Valley: a kind young toymaker kneels to hand a small wooden doll in a cloth dress to a richly dressed little girl in a silk coat, whose fine coach waits beyond the oak trees, while carved wooden animals line the workbench behind. Warm honeyed afternoon light with dappled green shade, tender storybook illustration.

blocks.text: Spring came softly to the Laughing Valley, and children walked for miles to see the toymaker. One bright morning a fine coach rolled up the lane, and out stepped a girl in a silk coat. Her name was Bessie Blithesome, and her father was a great lord of the south.

Claus shook his head gently. “You live in a palace,” he said. “Your shelves are full of pretty things.” But Bessie’s chin trembled, and her tears fell on the warm earth. “Pretty things are not the same as a friend,” she said.

Then Claus understood something new. Rich or poor, every child needs a friend to hold. He carved all afternoon under the oak tree. He made a little person with a smiling face and arms that could bend. Her dress was of the softest cloth.
Claus gives the first doll to Bessie Blithesome.
New word: doll — a small toy person, made to be loved.

Bessie held the doll as if it were made of morning light. “This is the best toy in the world,” she whispered. Claus bowed low, like a king in a story. And that was how the very first doll was born, in the Laughing Valley.

The news of the doll traveled from farm to town. Soon girls and boys alike sent their wishes to the valley, and Claus worked happily at his bench. He made rocking horses, little drums, and balls of leather. And in the evenings the ryls came to paint the cheeks of the dolls, red as berries. The knooks fetched pine wood from the deep forest. For the little folk of Burzee loved to help a friend who loved children. The more he gave away, the happier he grew.

chapters.title: Chapter 7 · Flossie and Glossie
chapters.artPrompt: A moonlit winter sky above sleeping snowy farms: two young deer with bright antlers leap upward through scattered stars hauling a small wooden sledge heaped with toy sacks, while a broad kindly toymaker in a fur-trimmed coat holds the reins and laughs into the wind. Silvery blue night warmed by golden sledge lanterns, joyful storybook illustration.

blocks.text: More and more letters came to the Laughing Valley, from children far away across rivers and mountains. Claus read them all by candlelight, and his heart ached. “My arms can carry only so much,” he sighed, “and my feet can walk only so far.”

So Claus went to the edge of Burzee and told Ak, the Master Woodsman. Ak smiled, for he had been waiting for these words. “Every child in the world shall be remembered,” he said. “It is not good that some have joy and others have none.”

Ak led Claus into the deep forest, where two young deer stood waiting among the ferns. “This is Flossie, and this is Glossie,” said Ak. “They are strong and gentle, and the knooks have taught them a secret: the way to run upon the wind.”
Flossie and Glossie learn to pull the sledge through the night sky.
New word: harness — the soft straps by which an animal pulls a sledge.

The knooks made a harness of the softest leather. The deer tossed their heads with joy. One moonlit night Claus climbed into the sledge, took the reins, and spoke a kindly word. Up leaped the deer — and the sledge rose above the treetops into the sky.

All night they flew, over sleeping farms and silver rivers, from one end of the land to the other. In the morning Claus came home tired and glad. Now, at last, no child was too far away, and the whole world had learned to wait for Santa Claus. From then on, Santa saved his longest journey for one night of the year — the night before Christmas. Then Flossie and Glossie flew faster than the wind, and the stockings of the world were filled by morning light.

chapters.title: Chapter 8 · The Helpers of the Night
chapters.artPrompt: A lamplit workshop at night: tiny knooks with kind furry faces carve wooden horses, delicate ryls paint cheeks and stars with flower-petal brushes, and stout gnomes hammer bright runners, while the toymaker sleeps folded in his chair behind them and finished toys gleam on every shelf. Amber firelight against deep blue night, busy cozy storybook illustration.

blocks.text: Now the whole world knew the name of Santa Claus, and letters came by the basketful. There were more children than ever, in more towns than Claus could count. He worked from dawn to dusk, but there were never enough toys. He could not bear to leave any wish unanswered.

The fire had burned down to red embers. One evening Claus fell asleep at his bench, with a half-carved horse still in his hand. And that night, a strange and wonderful thing happened. The little folk of Burzee crept quietly in at the door and set to work.

The knooks carved wood, for they know every tree and its kindness. The ryls painted cheeks and stars and stripes, for they know every color that flowers wear. The gnomes hammered hinges and bright runners, for they know the metals hidden under the ground.
The knooks and ryls work quietly at the bench by night.
New word: ryl — a tiny fairy of the flowers, who knows all their colors.

In the morning Claus woke and rubbed his eyes. The bench was covered with finished toys, and the little folk stood in a shy row by the door. “The children of the world are our children too,” they said. “We will help you always.” Claus thanked them with all his heart. And the fairies, who love children, flew ahead of the sledge each night. They found houses that no map had ever named. So no child was missed, however far away.

From that night on, the workshop never stood still. While Claus slept, the toys grew and grew in number, and every one was made with love. For that is the secret of all good gifts: the hands may be many, but the heart is one. And so it has been ever since.

chapters.title: Chapter 9 · The Great Battle
chapters.artPrompt: A stormy twilight battlefield at the forest’s edge: a tall white-bearded Master Woodsman with a great staff stands radiant before ranks of fairies, knooks, ryls and gnomes holding lamps of light, while a swarm of shadowy goblin-like Awgwas recoils before the glow, darkness breaking apart like smoke. Dramatic violet-and-gold contrast, brave but not frightening, storybook illustration.

blocks.text: Far away in their dark caves, the Awgwas grew angrier and angrier. They hated laughter. They hated toys, and kindness, and children singing. Everywhere they crept, songs ended. And most of all, they hated Santa Claus, who carried joy across the world.

Now they did more than hide the toys. They laid snares on the sledge roads. They whispered bad dreams into children’s ears. They tried with all their wicked tricks to stop the gifts from ever reaching the world. Even the deer trembled at the snares.

So Ak rose up from Burzee, and the fairies and knooks and ryls and gnomes rose with him. “A world without joy is no world at all,” he said. Then came the great battle between good and evil, such as the forest had never seen.
Ak and the immortals of Burzee stand fast against the Awgwas.
Ask your child: the Awgwas hated joy. What made them lose in the end?

The Awgwas came swarming with their shadows, but the light of the immortals was stronger. Fairies shone, knooks struck, and the wicked tricks broke like thin ice. At last the darkness broke and fled, and the Awgwas were seen no more in all the world.

Santa Claus did not fight, for his hands were made for making, not hurting. He sat in the valley with the children’s letters on his knee, waiting and hoping. He trusted his friends, and his friends did not fail. And when the news came, he opened his workshop wide, and there was work for all. After that, nothing in the world could stop the toys. The sledge flew on the darkest and stormiest nights, for no shadow was left to fear. And the stockings were filled every Christmas Eve, in every land where children sleep.

chapters.title: Chapter 10 · When the World Grew Old
chapters.artPrompt: A quiet fireside interior at night: an old white-bearded toymaker sits musing in his chair by a low fire, an unfinished wooden toy resting on his knee, stockings hanging empty on the mantel and sacks of letters stacked beside him, while snow drifts past the small window. Soft ember-orange glow against winter blue, gentle reflective storybook illustration.

blocks.text: The years rolled by like clouds, and Santa Claus worked on. His beard turned silver, and his hands grew slow. But his eyes were as kind as ever, and no child was ever turned away. Still he smiled at every letter.

The world grew old too, and busier than before. Men hurried and counted and worried, and many forgot how to play. But the children still believed. They still hung their stockings. And so the world stayed young where it mattered.

One winter night, Claus sat by his fire and counted his years. “I am getting old,” he said to the little flames. “Soon I shall not be able to make the journey. Who will fill the stockings then?” The fire cracked, and gave no answer.
Old Santa Claus sits by his fire, wondering who will fill the stockings.
Ask your child: Santa is growing old. Who do you think will help him?

But far away in Burzee, the immortals had heard. Ak the Master Woodsman called a great council. All the folk of the forest came: the fairies, the nymphs, the knooks, the ryls, and the gnomes. Each one loved him in their own way.

Necile came too, the nymph who had found a baby in the moss long ago. “He was given to us as a child,” she said softly. “We cannot let the world take him back.” And every immortal in the hall nodded. So it was decided. The Mantle of Immortality was brought out from its long keeping. It was woven of light that never fades. It would be placed on the shoulders of the one man who gave away everything he made. No one else had ever earned it. And that man was Santa Claus.

chapters.title: Chapter 11 · The Mantle of Immortality
chapters.artPrompt: A snowy grove at the edge of the Laughing Valley at midnight: a ring of radiant immortals — the tall Master Woodsman, gentle nymphs, fairies and knooks — lay a mantle of woven starlight across the shoulders of an old toymaker asleep in his chair, the light rising softly around them like snowfall glowing upward. Silver and pale gold on deep blue, solemn and tender storybook illustration.

blocks.text: On a still winter night, the immortals came softly to the Laughing Valley. Ak walked in front, tall as the trees, and Necile walked beside him. They found Santa Claus asleep in his chair, an unfinished toy upon his knee. The valley lay silent under a coat of new snow.

They did not wake him. They gathered round him in a ring, and Ak lifted the Mantle of Immortality from its case of woven light. “This friend of children has given everything away,” said Ak. “Tonight the world shall give something back.” Necile stood among them, and her eyes were shining.

They laid the Mantle gently on his shoulders, and it settled like snow, like starlight, like a mother’s arms. And Santa Claus opened his eyes, and understood at once. “For me?” he asked. “For you,” said Ak, “and for every child, for ever.” The Mantle weighed nothing and everything, as old stories tell.
The immortals lay the shining Mantle on Santa’s shoulders as he wakes.
New word: immortal — living for ever and ever, like the fairies of Burzee.

And Claus wept a little, for he was humble, and then he laughed, for he was glad. And all Burzee shone with happiness. “You gave all your gifts away,” said Ak, “and see — the world has given them back to you, a hundredfold.”

And so it goes on still. From that night, Santa Claus would never grow old. Each Christmas Eve, Flossie and Glossie and all their kin are harnessed to the sledge. The knooks load the sacks, and the ryls tie the last ribbons. Then the deer leap into the sky. If you listen, you may hear them passing over the rooftops. For Santa Claus remembers every child, for ever and ever.
